newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - Downside risk for New Zealand bond prices.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Downside risk for New Zealand bond prices.

text.p: By Jason Wong, Economist at First NZ Capital.

WELLINGTON, Nov 27 - While the bond market appears to be in a holding pattern at the moment, we've taken the opportunity to review New Zealand bond valuation and prospects for the future. We've churned through various models ranging from the very simple yield spread model (NZ 10 year rate less US 10 year rate) to more complex regression models that include inflation expectations, overseas bond yields, the economic cycle, and domestic monetary conditions.
Using these models, NZ bonds are currently around fair value to slightly expensive.
There are many positive valuation aspects of NZ bonds, but much of this good news is probably priced in.
Looking forward, there is potentially a downside risk to NZ's economic fundamentals, and we do not necessarily believe that the market has priced in this risk appropriately.
We therefore view the balance of risks for bond prices as being on the downside on a one year view.

Short-term, we are fairly neutral on NZ bonds. NZ bond yields have benefited from a global search for high yields and this momentum still exists, although given the recent narrowing of spreads this force should be waning.
Looking at the pluses and minuses for NZ bonds, there are many good reasons why NZ bonds appear to be attractive:
1. EASIER MONETARY POLICY.

Recent data suggests that there is scope for an easing in monetary policy in the near future. The outcome of coalition negotiations and implications of fiscal policy will be a key influence in determining the scope of the easing.
2. FALLING INFLATION.

This is related to (1) above. In the current cycle, annual underlying inflation has probably peaked (at 2.3 percent in the September quarter). Consensus forecasts are for inflation to average 1.5 percent over the next three years.
3. FISCAL SURPLUSES AND FALLING BOND SUPPLY.

NZ's superb fiscal situation means that the government's borrowing requirement is fast diminishing, reducing bond supply and placing downward pressure on yields. This has been a significant event for the NZ bond market and could mean that historical averages overstate fair value for NZ bond yields.
4. MODERATE GROWTH.

Although monetary policy will be easing through most of 1997, it will probably remain tighter than neutral for some time to come. Under such a scenario, there may be little prospect of growth far exceeding its potential rate.
5. HIGH RELATIVE YIELDS.
NZ bonds offer attractive high yields relative to oversesas markets.
Playing devil's advocate, one could argue against the rosy picture above in the following way:

1. The market has been anticipating easier monetary policy for some time now. The shape and slope of the yield curve suggests that much of the good news is already priced into bonds. Moreover, we believe that the balance of risks lie on the side of a delayed or slower rate of easing than expected.
2. Inflation prospects on a short-medium term view are good but there is a high chance that the Reserve Bank's inflation target will be widened and/or shifted upwards.

Under a 0 to 2 percent inflation target, underlying inflation has averaged 1.7 percent. Under a -1 to 3 percent target perhaps an average of 2.5 percent is likely, and higher still on a 0 to 3 percent target.

Has the market fully discounted this potential rise in NZ's long-run inflation rate? Shouldn't there be an added "credibility" premium if it appears that the policy targets agreement is changed so easily?

3. A very much scaled down bond issuance programme has been the effect of very large fiscal surpluses, but has the market discounted the possibility of a rising issuance programme to cover domestic maturities if fiscal surpluses are diminished under coalition government?
4. As Dr Brash mentioned in a recent speech, NZ short term interest rates have been out of sync with global rates as the NZ economy has taken longer to cool down to a non-inflationary growth rate.

NZ monetary policy could well be easing at a time when other countries are tightening policy, leading to the narrowing of spreads and triggering the fall in the NZ currency that most domestic economists expect.

On a purchasing power parity basis, NZ's currency is about 10 to 15 percent over-valued. Overseas investors' appetite for NZ dollar assets would soon be reduced if the potential currency risks begin to materialise.

Weighing up these risks, we believe that there is potential downside to the relative value of NZ bonds on a one year view. At current yields it would appear that no political risk premium has been built in.
NZ bonds have rallied and spreads have narrowed, even as it has become clearer that under a new government, NZ's economic fundamentals will probably deteriorate.

Short-term, we are fairly neutral on NZ bonds. NZ bond yields have benefited from a global search for high yields and this momentum still exists, although given the recent narrowing of spreads this force should be waning.
On November 12, the bond market got a taste of things to come when Winston Peters commented that a widened 0 to 3 percent inflation target was still "too narrow".
The 10 year bond rate sold off around 10 basis points. There are plenty more shocks like this in store as it becomes clearer that NZ's key economic fundamentals are at risk.
While there may not be any major policy changes under coalition government, there will be incremental (negative) changes across a wide range of variables.
If history is a good guide to the future then, based on our models, NZ bonds can expect to settle in a 7 to 7.5 percent range on a long-run average basis.
A key variable which will determine the long run average is NZ inflation expectations.

If the 0 to 2 percent inflation target survived the current political negotiating process, then inflation expectations over time would probably drift down towards the lower end of say, a 2 to 2.5 percent range. This would give an average fair value result just under 7 percent.

If, in addition, the forecast ongoing budget surpluses and tightening bond supply also survives the perils of coalition government (the probability is falling), NZ bond yields might surprise on the downside.
If the inflation target is widened or shifted upward, then there is the risk of higher inflation expectations and our estimate of fair value for NZ bonds would rise accordingly.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
